articles.title: UK survivor of Canadian poison seller says he exploited her despair
articles.summary: Elisabeth Belien tells Kenneth Law's sentencing hearing she took the poison when she was just 23 years old.
articles.byline: Dan Sales, Christina McSorley, Sean Dilley

blocks.text: A British woman, one of the survivors of Canadian poison seller Kenneth Law, faced him in court on Wednesday to describe how he had exploited her vulnerability.
Elisabeth Belien told the four-day sentencing hearing of Law in Ontario, Canada she had been at her lowest ebb when he sold her toxic chemicals when she was just 23.
Belien, who until Wednesday had not been known as one of his customers, said she had physically recovered after being successfully given an antidote by medics.
But as she faced him as he sat in the glass-panelled dock, she revealed she had suffered "survivor's guilt" after learning from police others had died.
Law has admitted 14 counts of aiding suicides in Canada after meeting people in suicide forums online. But there are almost 80 deaths in the UK that have also been linked to him.
As part of a plea deal with Canadian authorities, Law will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths.
But impact statements from their families are being read during the sentencing hearing this week.
Belien told the court: "I had struggled with my mental health for a long time before this. Kenneth Law made it a lot easier to act on that despair.
"I continue to struggle with intrusive thoughts and flashbacks of that day.
"I made a full recovery. However, emotionally and psychologically, the effects are far more long lasting.
"I feel guilty for surviving. Although I survived It has also impacted my loved ones. I feel like my vulnerability was exploited. I still feel a lot of shame about what happened.
"I felt like the purchasing from Kenneth Law, I enabled him to continue his business, supplying his products, to other people who might have been vulnerable, like I was. I felt guilty for surviving."
Belien, who said she took the poison in January 2023, said being in court reminded her "how easily" it could have been her own parents there talking about her.
"I'm learning that things can get better," she said.
"I'm learning to be excited to see what the future holds for me. But the gratitude I'm feeling for being alive today doesn't take away from the trauma of the experience."
Authorities say Law, a former chef, sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients he met in online suicide forums in 40 countries. Roughly a quarter of the packages were sent to the UK.
He was arrested in May 2023, following a complex investigation by at least 11 law-enforcement agencies that involved investigators from around a dozen countries, including the UK, Italy and the US.
David Parfett, whose son Tom died in October 2021, said in a victim impact statement: "Since Tom died, I've struggled with my mental health.

"Initially, in the months after he died, I didn't properly mourn him, because my focus was on understanding, and then exposing the harm caused by the internet platforms that allowed Law to trade suicide to kids.

"I'm still, after five years, unable to fully process Tom's death. I'm a very different person to who I was before Tom took his own life, having previously been gregarious, outgoing. I find it difficult to enjoy life."
A statement was also read from the parents of Henry Tucker, a 14-year-old British boy who died in October 2021.
Kate and Henry Tucker said Henry had been diagnosed with autism but actually had a neurological condition that could have been treated with antibiotics.
"The realisation that his suffering and his death could have been prevented is a weight that is impossible to bear," they said.
"The death of a children under these circumstance is a heavy burden to carry for the rest of our lives.
"We will carry it however with Henry's blessings until we meet again. We love you Henry."
Norson Harris, the father of British victim Ashleigh Harris, read a statement in person on the agony of losing his daughter.
He said: "The circumstances of Ashleigh's death have been incredibly tough to bear.
"We all feel we should have been able to prevent Ashleigh's death.
"Rather than offer the help needed that individual Kenneth Law sold her a chemical that Ashleigh took to end her life.
"I still hope over time Mr Law will recognise the answer to Ashleigh and the myriad of others who reached out to him should have been that they were loved and there was help available to them."
Earlier Stephen Mitchell Sr, the father of Canadian Stephen Mitchell Jr, told of the aftermath of his death on March 25 2023.
"He was ill, he needed help, and I tried my best to bring him that help," he said.
"Mr Law robbed my son of that chance to be well."
Mr Mitchel Sr, addressing Law in court, said: "I'm willing to accept that during Mr Law's time in incarceration, he might have had brief moments of regret, or even despair and helplessness.
"Perhaps he may have even thought during those moments: my life is meaningless, what is the point of living.
"That was the same thoughts that my son Stephen had before he took the chemicals that Mr Law sold him.
"When my son was well, he would have gladly helped Mr Law work out his depressive thoughts, if asked, because he believed in the value of people."
Sandra Scott, whose daughter, Amara Scott, died on February 9 2022 aged 25, said she and her family were trying to help her through a mental health crisis.
"Our efforts were cut short when, in her most vulnerable state, she made contact with the accused, she said.
"The day I and her friends found Amara, and the way that she died – it broke my heart.
"It was a blessing and an honour to be Amara's mother."
The hearing continues.
If you or anyone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this article, details of organisations offering information are available at BBC Action Line

articles.title: Democrats accuse Susan Collins of corruption after bombshell ‘pay-to-play’ report
articles.summary:
Republican senator calls bribery allegation ‘categorically false’ as ProPublica reports Trump derailed FBI inquiry

Democrats in Maine on Wednesday accused Republican senator Susan Collins of…

blocks.text: Democrats in Maine on Wednesday accused Republican senator Susan Collins of corruption after a major media outlet reported that the FBI had proposed investigating her for allegedly accepting bribes – before Donald Trump derailed the inquiry.

The article from the investigative newsroom ProPublica rocked the race for Collins’s Senate seat, which is crucial to Democrats’ hopes of winning control of the chamber in the 3 November midterm election. The outlet reported that in the run-up to Collins’s successful bid for a fifth term in 2020, the head of her Super Pac had solicited a campaign donation from contracting firm Navatek, which demanded assurances of business from the government in return.

Using a shell company, Navatek CEO Martin Kao later sent $150,000 to the Super Pac, then told other executives he had been informed Collins would ensure the firm won $32m in federal contracts. In late 2024, the FBI was moving towards investigating the arrangement, in what would have been a large-scale political bribery inquiry, but the agents leading the case were pushed out amid a wider purge of the bureau Trump ordered after returning to power last year, while a justice department office that oversees investigations of politicians was gutted.
Collins has disputed the report, which her deputy chief of staff Annie Clark called “categorically false” and noted that Kao is currently in federal prison after pleading guilty to fraud charges.
But it served as grist for Maine Democrats who hope they can finally convince voters to unseat Collins, who has represented the state since 1997 and survived repeated re-election challenges.
“This is corruption of the highest order,” said Troy Jackson, the former state senate president and the Democratic nominee to take on Collins this year.
“We deserve answers about every contract and every conversation that Collins and her team facilitated on the backs of taxpayers. The jig is up.”

Collins is the only Republican running for re-election in a state Kamala Harris won in 2024, but has a history of being a tenacious opponent. The last time Collins was on the ballot, in 2020, she beat her Democratic opponent Sara Gideon by eight percentage points, even as Joe Biden carried the state in the presidential race.
Political forecasters consider her re-election campaign to be a toss-up, though recent polls have shown Jackson narrowly ahead.

At a Wednesday press conference in Portland, the largest city, state Democratic party executive director Devon Murphy-Anderson accused the senator of misconduct as chair of the Senate appropriations committee, a powerful role that oversees federal spending and which Collins has used to channel significant investment to her state.

“We sent Susan Collins to Washington to fight for us. Instead, it appears that she has sold us out yet again and gotten bailed out of trouble by the president of the United States,” Murphy-Anderson said.
“It is not the first time that she has betrayed us. However, this November we have the opportunity to ensure that it is one of the last.”

Addressing reporters separately, Collins’s campaign manager, Steve Abbott, denounced ProPublica’s reporting as based on “allegations from a guy who was awaiting sentencing for a significant federal offense who was trying to get his sentence reduced, as the article states directly”.
He said that the justice department under Joe Biden had absolved the senator of the “pay-to-play” scheme that Democrats accuse her of.

“In order for that claim to be true, you would have to disbelieve the Biden-led Department of Justice and the Biden-led FBI, who both investigated those contributions and the claims against Senator Collins, her campaign, and her federal staff, thoroughly, and found no basis to charge them,” Abbott said.

Maine lies at the center of Democrats’ plans for retaking control of the Senate from Republicans, who won a 53-seat majority in the 2024 election. Beyond Maine, Democrats hope to win in at least three other states currently held by Republicans that voted for Trump two years ago, while also defending seats in Georgia, Michigan, and New Hampshire.

Lance Dutson, a strategist who worked on Collins’s three most recent re-election campaigns, said the senator’s campaign in 2020 was so well-funded he found it “obviously absurd” that $150,000 would be viewed as a meaningful donation to her Super Pac.
“In 2020, by the end of that race, campaigns were struggling to find places to spend money,” said Dutson, who is not involved with Collins’s re-election effort this year.
He condemned ProPublica’s story as “a partisan hit piece” but said: “It’s definitely not helpful to have a story implying corruption show up in the newspaper in late September of an election year.”

While Dutson argued the report is not a “silver bullet” for Collins’s foes, he warned that Trump’s low approval ratings – which have unnerved Republicans nationwide – present a significant complication for the senator’s re-election.

“The headwind from Trump is very strong, as you know, and people are very upset about it,” he said. “This race is going to come down to Maine voters deciding whether that national argument is more important than the the direct relationship and the positive impact that Collins has had over the state.”

articles.title: Anthony Albanese says OpenAI agent hacked Medicare and he expressed ‘extreme concern’ to Sam Altman
articles.summary: Prime minister says he expressed ‘disappointment’ to chief executive it had taken the company ‘way too long’ to inform his government about the breach

blocks.text: Anthony Albanese says an artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI hacked Medicare in June.
The prime minister made the comments at the UN summit in New York, saying it appeared no personal information had been accessed – though investigations were ongoing.
“Nonetheless, this situation is obviously unacceptable,” Albanese said.
“Today, I spoke with the CEO of OpenAI, Sam Altman, to express Australia’s extreme concern about this incident.
“And I also expressed my disappointment that it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred.”
Albanese said the OpenAI agent had gained unauthorised access into the public-facing Medicare statistics reporting service portal, which is administered by Services Australia.
The portal contains non-sensitive Medicare information relating to data and statistics, such as spending.
Albanese said the agent had accessed “public and non-public files”
“A forensic investigation, aided by the Australian Signals Directorate, is now under way to ascertain more information, including what other government systems were affected,” Albanese said.
He said there appeared to be no broader compromise to the Services Australia network.
“Evidence currently available is there is no broader compromise to the Services Australia network.”
The deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, said the government learned of the June breach “a couple of weeks ago” and ministers were informed last week.
Marles that the agent was non-human and called the breach a “very serious incident”.
“What we have seen is unauthorised access in to an Australian government website and that is completely unacceptable and we have made that clear to OpenAI.”
after newsletter promotion

Marles said the government had established a taskforce that will be led by the the Prime Minister and Cabinet’s department and working with the Australian Signals Directorate and the AI Safety Institute.
The agencies will “examine everything that’s occurred here and to understand how – what the AI agent did and how this incursion occurred and what the impact of it has been,” he said.
“We are working cooperatively with OpenAI in relation to that, but fundamentally, this is a very unacceptable situation.”
It comes just days after Albanese joined more than 20 other leaders in urging greater international safeguards to protect people from the risks of AI.
Chief executives of OpenAI and Anthropic are set to address the UN on AI safety today.
Comment has been sought from OpenAI.
More details soon…

articles.title: Three charged with assault after anti-migration protests in Hampshire
articles.summary:
Hundreds gathered on Tuesday night in anticipation of a small boat arriving in Gosport

Three people have been charged in connection with anti-migrant protests which drew hundreds of…

blocks.text: Three people have been charged in connection with anti-migrant protests which drew hundreds of demonstrators to a marina in Hampshire on Tuesday night.
Six people were arrested by police, as anti-migrant activists who mistakenly believed a small boat was due to arrive at Gosport gathered in an attempt to disrupt the arrival of any asylum seekers.

Those charged are Shannon Dodds, 32, of Leonard Road in Gosport, who has been charged with two counts of assault by beating of an emergency worker, Sally Pearson, 31, of Forton Road in Gosport, who has been charged with assault by beating of an emergency worker and a racially aggravated public order offence, and Toby Matthews, 33, of Forton Road in Gosport, who has been charged with common assault of an emergency worker.
Dodds and Pearson have been remanded in custody and will appear at Portsmouth magistrates court on Thursday 24 September.
Matthews was bailed but must appear at Portsmouth magistrates court on 9 November.
More details soon …

articles.title: In a first, olive ridley turtles spotted nesting on California’s beaches
articles.summary:
Scientists are questioning whether the nestings on Seal and Huntington Beach were freak occurrences or start of a trend

A sea turtle crawled out of the surf in southern California last…

blocks.text: A sea turtle crawled out of the surf in southern California last weekend around sunset and started laying eggs in the sand.

People on Huntington Beach who saw the female olive ridley sea turtle were shocked and excited. And they weren’t the only ones freaking out, said Justin Viezbicke, the California stranding coordinator for the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Association (Noaa).
“This is the first documented case of a turtle nesting on the west coast,” Viezbicke said.

What made the sighting even more noteworthy is that two different olive ridley sea turtles were identified laying eggs on Orange county beaches in the last week, the first on Seal Beach and the second on Huntington Beach. It’s a pattern that has scientists questioning whether the nestings are a freak occurrence, or the beginnings of a more lasting trend.

While early news reports suggested that a single female turtle laid eggs on both California beaches, scientists further analyzed photographs of the turtles’ shell shape and barnacle patterns and determined that two separate olive ridley turtles had begun nesting on the US coast, Viezbicke said.
Olive ridley turtles typically lay their eggs on beaches much further to the south, in Mexico and Central America, Viezbicke said.

What caused the turtles to begin nesting further north than usual is the “million dollar question”, he said. Scientists are examining several different theories, including the environmental factor of warmer coastal waters, to other effects of El Niño, or whether the turtles “could have been blown off course by the recent hurricane”.
“There’s been a lot of activity in the Pacific Ocean,” Viezbicke said.

While it’s too soon to tell, it’s also possible that these first recorded US coastal nests could herald a broader northward shift in the olive ridley turtle’s nesting patterns, one driven by climate crisis and the warming ocean waters in the turtles’ native nesting areas, said Lance Adams, an aquarium veterinarian at the Aquarium of the Pacific in Long Beach.

The sex of the olive ridley turtle is determined by temperatures where the eggs hatch, and warmer temperatures produce more female turtles. “After about 87.8F, they’re almost all female,” Adams said. To achieve a balanced population, the sea turtles might need access to cooler nesting areas.
On the other hand, it’s hard to generalize from just two sightings, Adams said: “The turtles could be here by mistake.”

Because the nesting season is not over and individual olive ridley turtles typically lay multiple nests of eggs, “We might see additional sea turtles making beach crawls to nest in the next 30 to 90 days,” Adams said.
For protection, the new turtle nests have been surrounded by fencing. But there’s only so much local officials can do to protect the eggs, which typically take 45 to 60 days to hatch, Viezbicke said.

It’s not just the dangers from local predators, such as coyotes, or from interfering humans. New hurricane swells and high tides are expected as soon as Monday of next week, Viezbicke said – and there’s a risk of the extreme weather “washing away that part of the beach”.

Californians who spot sea turtles on a local beach should not interfere with them, and should keep at least 50 ft away, Adams, the aquarium veterinarian, advised. To advise authorities of a new turtle sighting, tell a lifeguard, or call Noaa’s marine animal stranding hotline, he recommended.

Getting close to the turtles’ fenced-off nesting spots is not a good idea, he said: “People won’t see anything.” If locals want to observe live sea turtles in action, they can visit rescued turtles on display in rehabilitation tanks at an aquarium.
Olive ridley sea turtles are one of the most abundant turtle species worldwide, but are protected under the US endangered species act.

Warmer ocean temperatures have led to sightings of all kinds of sea creatures that aren’t typically spotted on the California coast, he noted, including different shark species, rays, sea horses and the venomous yellow-bellied sea snake.
People should aim to adapt to shift in wildlife patterns, and, in general, keep their distance, Adams said, though new unexpected species present different potential risks.
“Turtles aren’t particularly dangerous to humans. They can bite. They can slap with their flippers. Someone could potentially get hurt, but probably not seriously,” he said.

blocks.text: MLB·New

After playing Game 7 of the World Series last fall, the 2025 American League champion Toronto Blue Jays were officially eliminated from post-season contention with Wednesday's 4-2 loss to open a doubleheader against the hometown Baltimore Orioles.
Score twice, go 1-for-14 with runners in scoring position vs. Orioles in 81st loss

A Toronto offence that struggled to score runs for much of the 2026 campaign went 1-for-14 with runners in scoring position and left eight men on base Wednesday. The Blue Jays saw their season record slip to 77-81 with four games remaining.
Pete Alonso paced the Orioles offence with his 41st home run of the season and former Blue Jays starting pitcher Chris Bassitt took a shutout into the sixth inning.
More to come.

articles.title: Belleville, Ont., police officer wounded in shooting near synagogue faces 'long, difficult road,' wife says
articles.summary: The wife of the police officer wounded in Sunday evening's shootout near a Belleville synagogue is speaking out about what she's calling "the scariest and darkest day" of her family's life.

image.caption: Const. Jeff Smith of the Belleville Police Service is seen in a family portrait shared on his wife's Facebook page. Smith was injured in a shooting outside a synagogue Sunday night and is recuperating in the hospital. His alleged attacker, Sean Ward, has died, investigators said Tuesday. (Ashley Smi

blocks.text: Ottawa·New
The wife of the police officer wounded in Sunday evening's shootout near a Belleville synagogue is speaking out about what she's calling "the scariest and darkest day" of her family's life.
Jeff Smith was outside a Jewish synagogue when a suspect fired on him, investigators say
The wife of the police officer wounded in Sunday evening's shootout near a Belleville, Ont., synagogue is speaking out about what she's calling "the scariest and darkest day" of her family's life.
"I don’t know where to begin," Ashley Smith, the wife of Const. Jeff Smith of the Belleville Police Service, wrote in a Facebook update dated Tuesday night.
"My words aren’t strong or steady yet, but I knew I needed to find them. I needed to use my voice for my dear Jeff, until he is able to use his," she wrote.

A Yom Kippur service was getting underway inside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue shortly after 7 p.m. Sunday when a suspect later identified as Sean Ward allegedly opened fire on Smith with a shotgun, according to the Belleville Police Service and Ontario's Special Investigations Unit (SIU).
Smith had been stationed outside the synagogue, which had requested police protection.

Precisely what happened before Smith was shot at is not yet known. The SIU — the civilian agency that investigates police conduct during shootings and other serious incidents in Ontario — is focused on what led Smith and a second officer to fire their weapons.
The Belleville Police Service will look into Ward's motives, Kristy Denette, an SIU spokesperson, said Monday.
Ward, 29, from nearby Quinte West, died following the incident, the SIU confirmed on Tuesday. He got as close as half a block to the synagogue, according to Denette.

Norm Weddum, the synagogue's president, said one of the building's street-facing windows was left with several bullet holes. Dozens of bullets also damaged nearby homes and vehicles, according to investigators.

items: 'This is not going to stop us,' Belleville, Ont., synagogue president vows after shooting incident
Suspect, police officer wounded in shooting outside Belleville, Ont., synagogue ID'd

blocks.text: Yom Kippur is the holiest day of the Jewish year.

"This was clearly a targeted attack against Jews gathering together to pray and be in community," the synagogue said in a statement issued Wednesday. "Jews must be able to gather, pray and live openly in our communities without fear.
"We will not allow fear to define our community."
'Life-saving' hands

In her Facebook post — which CBC News verified through a family friend — Ashley Smith thanked the "life-saving" and "steady, capable" hands of first responders and hospital staff, including "an angel neurosurgeon."
She also expressed gratitude to neighbours, friends, community members and volunteers.
"And then there are the hands that held me and my sweet girls when we were living through the scariest and darkest day of our lives," she wrote.
"Today, I held Jeff’s hand. And I thought about all of those hands."
Read Ashley Smith's full post below:
Sons of Jacob Synagogue has hailed Smith as a hero and said in its statement Wednesday that "our prayers are with [him] his family, his colleagues and everyone supporting his recovery."
"We will never know what might have happened inside our synagogue had Const. Smith not been there," the synagogue added.
Smith's wife wrote in her post that "every scared soul who was there on Sunday night" was in her family's prayers.
Smith has been with the Belleville Police Service since 2013.

The force's deputy chief, Sheri Meeks, said Monday that Smith is "a long-standing and highly respected member of our emergency response unit, known by his colleagues as a dedicated officer, trusted teammate and committed public servant."
Sunday's shooting incident is also a reminder of the reality of policing, she added.

"The men and women who wear this uniform are not just police officers," she said, her voice cracking. "They are parents, spouses, children, friends and neighbours. Every day they leave their homes and love ones not knowing what they may encounter. Yet when danger arises, they step forward to protect others."

articles.title: Cineplex may be going up for sale, company says in announcement of new CEO
articles.summary: Cineplex is considering a potential sale, the company revealed in a statement announcing former Landmark Cinemas head Bill Walker as its new CEO. While it said the board is confident in the company’s…

image.caption: In an announcement revealing Bill Walker as Cineplex's new CEO, the company said it is also undergoing a strategic review, and that selling the company may be part of its future. (Carlos Osorio/Reuters)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

Cineplex is considering a potential sale, the company revealed in a statement announcing former Landmark Cinemas head Bill Walker as its new CEO. While it said the board is confident in the company’s future prospects, it is evaluating all avenues.
Cineplex board initiates strategic review, says sale is one of 'a range of alternatives'

Cineplex is considering a potential sale, the company revealed in a statement announcing former Landmark Cinemas head Bill Walker as its new CEO, adding that while the board is confident in the company's future prospects, it is evaluating all avenues.
"The Board has initiated a Strategic Review to evaluate opportunities to enhance and maximize value for all shareholders," a memo on Walker's appointment said Wednesday.
"As part of the Strategic Review, the Board will consider a range of alternatives, including, but not limited to, a potential sale of the Company."
Goldman Sachs and TD Securities have been engaged as co-financial advisers for the strategic review, the company says.

According to Cineplex, the company is the largest cinema chain in Canada, operating more than 1,600 movie screens across nearly 170 movie theatres nationwide, and employing more than 10,000 people in its theatres and entertainment venues.
The last time Cineplex was up for sale was in 2019, when the company agreed to a $2.8-billion buyout by U.K.-based Cineworld Group PLC. However, the deal fell through.
Former CEO Ellis Jacob will serve as a special adviser to the board during the strategic review.
Phyllis Yaffe, chair of Cineplex's board, said that Cineplex has a "strong market position [and] portfolio of leading entertainment assets."
"However, we believe the Company's current market valuation may not fully reflect the strength of its business and long-term prospects," Yaffe said.
Walker previously led Landmark Cinemas, Canada's second-largest theatre exhibitor, and oversaw its sale to Kinepolis in 2017.

He said in the statement that he supported the strategic review, and that "regardless of the outcome," his focus would be on "driving operational excellence, delivering exceptional guest experiences and superior outcomes for shareholders."

Follow the day’s news live

blocks.text: Anthony Albanese says OpenAI agent hacked Medicare
Anthony Albanese has revealed an artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI hacked Medicare in June.
The prime minister made the comments at the UN summit in New York.

double quotation markThis incident occurred in June this year and involved an Open AI agent gaining unauthorised access into the public-facing Medicare statistics reporting service portal, which is administered by Services Australia. The AI agent accessed both public and non-public files. A forensic investigation, aided by the Australian Signals Directorate, is now under way to ascertain more information, including what other government systems were affected. The Medicare statistics reporting portal is a public-facing statistics portal that contains non-sensitive Medicare information relating to data and statistics, such as spending. No personal information is believed to have been accessed at this stage but investigations are ongoing. Evidence currently available is there is no broader compromise to the Services Australia network. Nonetheless, this situation is obviously unacceptable. Today, I spoke with the CEO of Open AI, Sam Altman, to express Australia’s extreme concern about this incident. And I also expressed my disappointment that it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred.
Key events

blocks.text: PM to say Indo-Pacific ‘not a chessboard’ for superpowers

While Australia had ties with the US and China as its key security and trading partners respectively, Albanese will say the competition between the two powers should not be the only lens the Pacific should be dealt with.
“The Indo-Pacific is not a chessboard on which superpowers move the pieces,” he will say.
“Its countries are not spectators, they are shaping its future and writing their own script.”

The prime minister will make the speech after receiving the Atlantic Council’s Global Citizen award, where he is being recognised for his role in deepening alliances and promoting security and stability in the Indo-Pacific.
He will be among four award recipients at the event, including Formula One boss Stefano Domenicali, the president of Finland, Alexander Stubb, and actor Cynthia Erivo.
The speech comes a day after Albanese met briefly with Donald Trump at a gala dinner hosted by the American leader.
The prime minister and Trump have issued divergent calls on whether to rein in the use of AI after safety fears or, in the case of the US leader, accelerate its rollout.
World order no longer fit for purpose, says Albanese

The international world order set up following the second world war is no longer fit for the present-day environment, the prime minister will declare in a major foreign policy speech in New York today, Australian Associated Press reports.
In an address to the Atlantic Council, Anthony Albanese will say many of the institutions that were necessary post-1945 were not enough to meet present-day challenges.

The prime minister will use the speech on the sidelines of the United Nations general assembly in New York to argue partnerships with alliances remain crucial in a rapidly changing global environment.

double quotation markSince the end of the cold war, the prevailing assumptions of international affairs were clear: openness was security, efficiency mattered more than resilience and international rules would be observed. Those assumptions rested on the expectation that the influence of the major democratic powers would remain largely unchallenged. The post-1945 world order is no longer fit for purpose. Universal institutions that remain necessary are now not always sufficient for the challenges we face.
The prime minister will say Australia needed to shape a world order that will replace the old one, while preserving diplomatic rules.
Albanese will point to the strategic competition between the United States and China in the Indo-Pacific region as being the most consequential issue facing the region.

blocks.caption: Patrick Commins

blocks.text: Patrick Commins
OECD says Australia will struggle to get underlying inflation below 3%
The OECD says Australia will struggle to bring underlying inflation back below 3% in 2027, despite sub-par economic growth in this year and the next.

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development in its interim economic outlook flagged that the world economy had, once again, proved more resilient than expected to the global energy shock triggered by the ongoing Iran war.

The artificial intelligence boom had papered over many of the cracks, the report said, adding that “global economic prospects remain heavily dependent on whether a durable resolution to the Middle East conflict is achieved”.

With fuel costs here jumping over recent weeks and inflation proving more persistent than hoped, there is a strong consensus that the Reserve Bank will deliver another interest rate hike next Tuesday – the fourth this year.
The OECD projected Australia’s headline inflation would drop from 4.1% this year, to 2.8% in 2027.
But “core” inflation – which removes the effects of big price swings, like for fuel – would prove harder to shift back into the RBA’s 2-3% target range.
The OECD expected the underlying price growth measure to ease from 3.5% in 2026 to 3.1% in 2027.

“Faced with renewed energy price shocks and stronger than expected demand pressures, and at a time when inflation is already above target in many economies, central banks need to ensure that underlying inflation pressures are durably contained,” the OECD said.
Welcome
Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it will be Nick Visser with the main action.

articles.title: Trump's Board of Peace unveils $2.45bn plan to begin Gaza's reconstruction
articles.summary: The figure was announced during a meeting of the group's board at the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace has announced a Gaza recovery plan worth $2.45 billion (£1.85 billion) during a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
The funding will be spread across 66 programmes over six months, and directed at housing, diesel generation and waste removal, among other needs.

But the board admitted substantial donations were still needed, with $18bn pledged but only $280 million handed over so far. The board estimates full recovery and reconstruction will require about $71.4bn over the next decade.
Jared Kushner, Gaza Executive Board member and Trump's son-in-law, conceded the project faced "different delays on different things, for whatever reason".
"The goal of today was really just to show you that we're really fully committed to doing it," he told the meeting of board members and stakeholders.
He was joined in New York by US envoy Steve Witkoff, who said the group had made "real progress" over the past year.

"All of the hostages are home. There is a ceasefire, imperfect as it may be, but it still exists. Humanitarian efforts have achieved historic results, with billions of dollars donated and pledged to meet urgent needs and support the long work of recovery," Witkoff added.

In addition to fundraising, the plan faces significant challenges including how to ensure security for those operating in Gaza, overhaul internal governance and find consensus between Israeli and Palestinians officials.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told a separate press conference on Wednesday that "a number of countries have stepped forward and pledged financial assistance" and the board was "looking for more that will participate in that".
In August, a senior official on the Board of Peace, Nickolay Mladenov, criticised Israel's continuing air strikes on Gaza, as well as the actions of the Palestinian armed group Hamas.
In August, Mladenov warned that a collapse of last October's ceasefire would be "a point of no return" for the region.

At least 1,381 Palestinians, including 300 children, have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the US-brokered ceasefire began, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The Israeli military says five of its soldiers have been killed in combat since the ceasefire and one contractor was killed in an "operational accident".
The Board of Peace was created as part of Donald Trump's 20-point Gaza peace plan, which he unveiled alongside Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in September last year.

Hamas agreed to return all 48 remaining hostages being held in Gaza in exchange for Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails and Gaza detainees, and to the idea of handing over the governance of Gaza to Palestinian technocrats.
In July, Hamas said it had accepted a disarmament plan for Gaza which will see it lay down its arms, provided Israel ends "all forms of aggression" and withdraws its forces from Gaza.
But that was later rejected by Netanyahu, who said the military would stay in Gaza until Hamas is "genuinely" disarmed.
The Board of Peace was originally thought to be an international organisation intended to bring peace to Gaza, but later expanded to include conflicts worldwide.

articles.title: Drivers showed off their parallel parking chops in Pittsburgh. The winner did it in 6 seconds
articles.summary: Parallel parking is a driving skill that can be hard to master. Dan Leber founded Pittsburgh’s Parallel Parking Championship in 2021. Now hundreds of drivers participate in the low-stakes, silly…

image.caption: Clay Hartley won the 2026 Pittsburgh Parallel Parking Championship. He parked his vehicle in just six seconds impressing the judges. (Submitted by Dan Leber)

blocks.text: As It Happens

Parallel parking is a driving skill that can be hard to master. Dan Leber founded Pittsburgh’s Parallel Parking Championship in 2021. Now hundreds of drivers participate in the low-stakes, silly competition.
Pittsburgh’s Parallel Parking Championship is silly, competitive fun, organizer says
LISTEN | Parallel parking competitions are a thing:
As It Happens5:30Drivers showed off their parallel parking chops in Pittsburgh. The winner did it in 6 seconds
Parallel parking is perhaps among many people’s least favourite part about driving. But Dan Leber loves it.
So much so, that he founded and organized the Pittsburgh Parallel Parking Championship. His first event in 2021 drew around 30 participants. This year, nearly 200 people competed.

The idea of watching other people park might sound mundane, but Leber says it’s more exciting than it seems. At the event, participants drive their vehicles into a parallel-parking space and are assigned points for accuracy, speed, and style.
To make things more interesting, Leber and his wife's vehicles are used as markers for drivers to park between. They've been damaged before, but Leber says he's not precious about it.
Hate parallel parking? Here's how the pros do it
Other cities have got in on the action as well, with competitions taking place in Portland and Philadelphia.
Leber says he’s proud he helped create a low-stakes, but fun way for adults to compete against each other. He spoke to As It Happens host Nil Köksal about why he’s passionate about parallel parking.
Dan, what did Clay Hartley do to make him this year's Pittsburgh parallel parking champ?

He did a great job at parallel parking. The space is 20 feet, I think he parked in six seconds, which is remarkably quick. I feel like it was something like 10 or 12 centimetres to the curb, so it was an impressive job.
I thought I was pretty good, but six seconds is fast. Is that the fastest you've ever seen in all your years doing this?
No, six seconds isn't the fastest. I feel like the fastest is under four or five seconds.

The formula someone told me ages ago when I was first learning to drive made it much easier for me. If you can stay calm and the space is a little bit roomy. Do you have a formula that you tell people who are still nervous?

Not really. If people are interested, I kind of give away the secret to winning the contest, which is you have to be lined up and you get one shot. Like you need to whip the car in there, hope that you're within, say six or seven inches of the curb, and then stop. There are so many people who get close and then they put the car in drive and pull up a foot and try to turn in and it's like you just lost it.

items: Parallel Parking: A Dying Art

blocks.text: You mentioned how long your championship has been around. There are competitors now and I want to read you a quote from a recent article in Rodent Track. “Pittsburgh's championship is arguably the loosest run event, as it falls short of banning back-up cameras and parking sensors.” How do you respond to that description?

I think that's hilarious that you bring that quote up because I saw that. I am so proud that we are the first to do this and it kind of originated in Pittsburgh. It's really fun to see how it evolves in other cities because each competition is different. But truthfully, I totally disagree with that sentiment. One of the comments we get most often is people talking about technology in cars, like self-parking and back-up sensors and cameras, and the reality is, when you've seen 700 nearly cars park and you understand the flow of how that works.

It's so clear that the folks who rely on those car aids they don't do well, they don't win, they don't come in second place. It's because they just don't feel the car well enough to do it quickly enough. Certainly you can park well, but it's not gonna take you to the top. The extra time it would take and the efficiency that we would lose in having to cover cameras and explain to [competitors] turn all the stuff off is not worth it, and the truth is that it just doesn't help you.
It’s not an unfair advantage is what you’re saying. What is it that makes you love parallel parking so much? How do you explain that when people ask you why you would start this in the first place?
I think it's interesting for a couple reasons. First of all, it's so low consequence and it doesn't matter. It’s not whether you're good or not, it has no bearing on anybody as a person.
I don't know. Some people use it as a major point of pride.

Yeah, sure, certain people can. But also it's something that most people do a lot and as an adult, I feel like you are less apt to be involved in sports and competitive things. And it's a really silly competitive thing that I think at an individual level, everybody feels and acknowledges alone in a car when they do it. So the idea of taking it to a place where it's a competition among others is really interesting and fun. And again, it's just silly, it doesn't mean anything.
Any damage done to cars in the course of your six years of this competition?

Yeah, I mean damage is relative. We use my wife and my own car, front and back. Everybody comes in a good spirit and certainly some people go for it and the car has been hit, but not to cause any damage. Actually, this year was probably the wildest example of that. There was some guy in a mid-70s blue eight-foot Ford F-150 that was going for it and he somehow hit the curb and my van at the exact same time, which has never happened before.
And you're OK with that? Damage to your cars?
Yeah, they're not precious. Everything's fine.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Marcus Medford is an award-winning multimedia journalist based in Toronto. He's worked as a digital producer, chase producer and senior writer for CBC. He's also written for CTV News Channel and been a reporter for ByBlacks.com and NewCanadianMedia.ca. His interests include current affairs, politics, soccer and social issues. You can reach him with story ideas at Marcus.Medford-Kerr@cbc.ca.
Interview produced by Kevin Robertson

articles.title: Hacked FBI employee data contains sensitive information about intelligence roles
articles.summary: FBI data allegedly stolen by the hacking group ShinyHunters carries granular detail about ‌scores of bureau officials’ job assignments, including sensitive work against Chinese spies, Russian…

image.caption: FBI data allegedly hacked by a group known as ShinyHunters contains sensitive information about employees, including job assignments, Reuters has found. (Jenny Kane/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

FBI data allegedly stolen by the hacking group ShinyHunters carries granular detail about ‌scores of bureau officials’ job assignments, including sensitive work against Chinese spies, Russian intelligence, drug cartels and more, Reuters has found.
Reuters has found that data allegedly hacked by ShinyHunters has details about work against China, Russia

FBI data allegedly stolen by the hacking group ShinyHunters carries granular detail about ‌scores of bureau officials' job assignments, including sensitive work against Chinese spies, Russian intelligence, drug cartels and more, Reuters has found.

The 5,000-line spreadsheet — said by the hackers to represent only a small piece of their claimed two- to three-terabyte trove — includes names, addresses, telephone numbers, dates of birth, social security numbers, and emergency contact details for what they claimed were thousands of FBI employees.
It also includes details of assignments to specific field offices and, in some cases, ​to units engaged in high-stakes intelligence, security or counterespionage work.

In a statement, the FBI said ​it was aware of "a cyber-criminal enterprise group claiming a compromise of the FBIJobs.gov portal and alleged impact to FBI employee personally identifiable information."
The bureau said the cause of the breach was still undetermined, but that it was "actively and aggressively investigating the matter."

The hackers said on Tuesday ​that they had breached the FBI, stealing data on a large number of current and former FBI employees. ShinyHunters said it is holding ⁠the data hostage until the bureau rescinds an ⁠unflattering statement about the group issued in May.
'Foreign intelligence service goldmine'
Former FBI counterintelligence operative Eric O'Neill said the data ‌allegedly stolen by ShinyHunters was "a foreign intelligence service goldmine."
"China would be incredibly interested to know the individuals who are working against it," said O'Neill, who founded the cybersecurity company Nexasure AI after his stint at the bureau.
He predicted that other hostile intelligence services would be eager to get their hands on the data, along with disgruntled extremists in the United States.
"If I were on that list I would be very concerned," he said.

items: ShinyHunters hackers say they breached FBI, stole employee data

blocks.text: ShinyHunters said in ⁠a statement Wednesday that it was trying to keep the personnel information from circulating widely in the meantime.
"If the 5,000 sample data records leak, it's not because of us," the group said.

Although Reuters has not been able to authenticate the entire spreadsheet, it has been able to individually verify the details of more than 22 people by cross-referencing information in the hacked data ‌with credit records and previous data leaks carried by the dark web intelligence platform District 4 Labs.
Staffers listed China, Russia roles

Some of the assignment details in the ShinyHunters' data are indistinguishable from what employees themselves might say publicly, noting agents at field offices in Baltimore or Newark, New Jersey, for example. Others referred to publicly known bureau subdivisions such as the Internet Crime Complaint Center or the FBI academy at Quantico in Virginia.
But in some cases, the data referred ​to FBI units or initiatives that were sensitive or whose existence has not previously been disclosed.
The data names 14 staffers focused on China-related matters, including members of the "China criminal enterprise unit," the "China tech transfer analysis unit," and the "China intelligence section."
Online learning platform strikes deal with hackers that targeted schools | Hanomansing Tonight

Nine others ⁠are listed as serving in roles related to Russia, including two in the "Russia Operations Section" and one working on "Russia Critical Infra and Tech Threat." Three people are listed as working in ⁠Iran- or Hezbollah-focused intelligence roles.

Eighteen others are listed as working with "data intercept" or "telecom intercept" technologies, or in the FBI's "clandestine technical operations" unit, or its "covert access section," or in ⁠video, audio ⁠or electronic surveillance roles.
A further 11 FBI staffers are listed ​as working in HUMINT, or human intelligence jobs, including several listed as working in the "Humint program management section."

items: A cyberattack hit universities worldwide, including top Canadian schools. Here's what we know
Telus probes cybersecurity incident that 'ShinyHunters' group claims responsibility for

blocks.text: Trevor Hilligoss, a former army investigator who worked with the FBI, said the information ​tying specific named people to human intelligence work was ⁠particularly troubling.
"You don't have to look far to find examples of undercover agents being harmed when their cover is blown," he said.

Hilligoss, now the chief intelligence officer for cybersecurity company SpyCloud, said his concerns were heightened by the inclusion of emergency contacts — often spouses or children — "who may have less operational security knowledge than their relative that works in a sensitive field."

Reuters could not verify that all the job assignments were authentic or up-to-date, but it was able to match the career details or titles of eight people whose data was leaked to information in court filings, ⁠news articles, or public profiles on LinkedIn or to ‌online posts on sites such as Instagram.

articles.title: Berlin Airport briefly suspends flights over drone sighting
articles.summary: Airspace over the German capital was temporarily closed after a drone was spotted on the runway. Flights have resumed but are experiencing delays.

image.caption: https://gadebate.un.org/enImage: Michael Ukas/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Berlin's airport briefly suspended flights on Wednesday evening after a drone sighting, Germany's DPA news agency cited airport and police officials as saying.

A drone was spotted on the Berlin Brandenburg Airport's northern runway at 8:00 p.m. (1800 GMT). Airspace above the airport was closed minutes later and operations were suspended for at least 45 minutes.
Several flights were diverted to Dresden.
As of 9:05 p.m., airspace was reopened but flights were experiencing delays.
Drone sightings on the rise
Drone sightings have become a common occurrence for airports in Europe, with Berlin's airport recording the highest number of sightings in Germany in the first part of the year.

Some 28 drone sightings were recorded during the first six months, as per figures by the German air traffic control (DFS). In seven of those cases, flight operations at the airport were temporarily suspended.
This is an jump from last year, when eight drones were detected at the airport and its surroundings in the whole of 2025, according to DFS.

articles.title: ‘My friend’: Anthony Albanese announces $60m more for Ukraine at Zelenskyy meeting
articles.summary:
An emotional prime minister says that Kyiv’s cause is ‘an issue for the world’ as he also sets out the need for a new global order

Anthony Albanese has announced Australia will provide $60m…

blocks.text: Anthony Albanese has announced Australia will provide $60m more in support for Ukraine’s fight against Russia’s invasion during an emotional meeting with Volodymyr ⁠Zelenskyy on the sidelines of the UN meeting in New York.

With the prime minister planning to use a key speech in New York to warn that the international world order was “no longer fit for purpose”, he hugged the Ukrainian president as the latyter thanked Australia for its support.
Albanese became emotional as he paid tribute to his “friend” Zelenskyy in his fight against Russian aggression.
“[His] leadership has been, I think, quite extraordinary, leading people in circumstances which are extraordinarily difficult,” he said.
“Russia thought it could just steamroll through in a matter of weeks, and what we have found is that the people of Ukraine were underestimated.”
The two leaders signed a 10-year bilateral security agreement which will lead to an extra $45m in Australian Defence Force equipment for Ukraine.
A further $10m will go to Ukraine’s energy support fund, while $5m will be spent on humanitarian assistance.
The $60m fund will bring Australia’s total contribution to Ukraine since Russia’s invasion in 2022 to $1.9bn.

As part of the agreement, Australia will also step up training to help Ukrainian forces deter and repel any future Russian attacks. It will also look to explore co-operation for training centres and jointly produce air-defence measures, missiles and drones.
The prime minister said the agreement was a proud day for Australians in seeking to uphold international laws.
“This is an issue not just for Europe, this is an issue for the world,” Albanese told reporters in New York upon signing the agreement.

“If a large, more powerful country in Russia is allowed to profit from breaking the international rules of law with its illegal and immoral invasion of Ukraine, then that sets a bad precedent for the entire world.”
Albanese said the bilateral agreement would be in place not only during the war in Ukraine, but during peacetime once the conflict concludes.
Zelenskyy said the agreement was the “strongest document between our countries”, and would increase trade and security.
“It’s all for our people, for the security,” he said.

It was a busy day of diplomacy for Albanese, who was addressing the Atlantic Council with a major speech on foreign policy and also signed a new strategic partnership with the Netherlands, seeking to boost defence ties and secure justice for the victims of MH17.

In his speech, the prime minister was expected to say that the international world order set up following the second world war was no longer fit for purpose and that institutions that were necessary post-1945 were not enough to meet present-day challenges.

The prime minister will use the speech on the sidelines of the United Nations general assembly in New York to argue partnerships with alliances remain crucial in a rapidly changing global environment.

“Since the end of the cold war, the prevailing assumptions of international affairs were clear: openness was security, efficiency mattered more than resilience and international rules would be observed,” he will say.
“Those assumptions rested on the expectation that the influence of the major democratic powers would remain largely unchallenged.
“The post-1945 world order is no longer fit for purpose. Universal institutions that remain necessary are now not always sufficient for the challenges we face.”
Australian Associated Press also contributed to this report.

articles.title: How the ‘poisonous tide’ of disinformation stokes division and sows despair
articles.summary:
Whether produced by Russia, China or far-right influencers, deepfakes and disinfo are being used to spread deceitful narratives

Russian disinformation campaigns are varied in their…

blocks.text: Russian disinformation campaigns are varied in their falsehoods and strategies.
The narratives range from a deepfake Tom Cruise slamming the Paris Olympics to portraying a recent Russian attack on a train near the Ukraine-Poland border as a false-flag operation.
Some efforts are blatant deepfakes, such as stamping the BBC logo on a video wrongly blaming Ukraine for a deadly missile salvo on its own citizens in Kramatorsk four years ago.

The tactics evolve too, from disseminating deceitful narratives through the Telegram messaging platform to “poisoning” AI systems by littering the internet with false stories in the hope they will be regurgitated by chatbots.
It is systematic and Andy Burnham has seen enough, announcing a new anti-disinformation agency, the National Centre for Information Defence.

“We’re talking about an insidious campaign that reaches into people’s homes and twists what they feel about their own country and community – creating a narrative of decline, stoking division and sowing despair,” he said.
Experts say picking off individual examples is the wrong approach and Burnham is right to tackle what he describes as a “poisonous tide”.
Going after isolated examples of disinformation is a “losers’ game”, says Ned Mendez, head of research at Alliance4Europe, a nonprofit that analyses these destabilising threats.

“You can spend all your time looking for a TikTok or a post on X but it’s not an effective use of your day. It’s the infrastructure that is the problem, so this is a step in the right direction, going after the networks,” he says.

Sophie Williams-Dunning, a cyber analyst at the Royal United Services Institute (Rusi) thinktank, says there is now a “sophisticated ecosystem which exists to exacerbate provokable users for one reason or another”.

Although Burnham is targeting “hostile state information attacks” this ecosystem does not just include Russia, which likes to amplify “divisive content”, says Williams-Dunning. It also includes far-right influencers who immediately jump on social flashpoints like the Southport and Belfast riots and individuals simply looking to make money by producing highly engaging content riffing on disruption.

The Burnham announcement is “welcome, if overdue”, says Williams-Dunning, who adds that there will be an accompanying debate about free speech and the right level of government intervention. Inevitably, malign networks will amplify those free-speech concerns, she says.
It is not just Russia deploying information attacks. China and Iran have both used deepfake newscasters to advance their goals.

One recent study, conducted mostly in February by the Social Market Foundation, found that more than a quarter of posts on X that relate to news were misinformation, a third of which were anti-immigration or Islamophobic. The UK government defines misinformation as the inadvertent spread of false information, while disinformation is the deliberate creation and spread of falsehoods to create harm or disruption. The two can intertwine to highly disruptive effect.

Labour has become increasingly concerned about Russian disinformation affecting the UK. The Starmer government in May cited information warfare from Moscow when it warned Britain was “confronting an industrial-scale attack on the UK’s and our allies’ information environment, aimed at undermining our security and democratic systems”.

Earlier this year MPs on the foreign affairs select committee called for the creation of a national counter-disinformation centre, in a similar vein to Sweden’s Psychological Defence Agency and France’s Vigilance and Protection against Foreign Digital Interference service.

Experts said Burnham’s announcement at least shows the UK government catching up, although Keir Starmer’s administration showed an awareness of social media’s contribution to unrest by launching the National Internet Intelligence Investigations unit after the Southport disturbances. Operated by the police, it monitors social media to help local forces “manage public safety threats and risks”.

The UK government has been taking action prior to Burnham’s announcement, however. In May it sanctioned employees of the Social Design Agency and ANO Dialog, Russian entities which it said the Kremlin uses for large-scale interference campaigns.

One example is the Doppelgänger network, so-called due to its technique of imitating the appearance of established media organisations including Le Monde, the Guardian, Der Spiegel and Fox News. Other examples include the 2023 surge in reports of bedbug infestations in France, falsely blaming Ukrainian refugees. The disinformation leaked into the British press and the French government concluded the stories were being artificially amplified by Russian-linked social media accounts

One of the most longstanding misinformation campaigns has centred on the idea that London is “dangerous” and “lawless”. Analysis of Reddit accounts by King’s College London found the number of such posts rose from 874 in 2008 to 258,444 in 2024.

Robert Topinka, reader in digital media and rhetoric at Birkbeck, University of London, said Russia did not necessarily start such storylines, but enthusiastically amplified them. He cautioned that counter-disinformation efforts should not assume “people are just being fooled by some sort of outside actor”. Rather he said Russia tends to find a point of tension and then create more content around it.
“What really is happening is people are feeling like Britain is run-down – that’s the real source of it,” said Topinka.
AI is adding a new dimension. Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta says AI-generated content is now a “near-standard” part of disinformation campaigns.

The UK thinktank Demos recently highlighted a chatbot “poisoning” campaign where falsehoods published online by a discredited Russian organisation, including the bodies of deceased Ukrainian soldiers being processed into meat products, were repeated by chatbot models.
The National Centre for Information Defence will have a lot of work to do.

articles.title: Health Canada suspends licence to collect plasma at Winnipeg Grifols location
articles.summary: An embattled for-profit plasma centre in Winnipeg is now officially suspended from collecting the blood component, after Health Canada cited concerns about its "quality management" in the wake of a…

image.caption: The Grifols location at 693 Taylor Ave. in Winnipeg. A Health Canada inspection in June found several deficiencies there. (Jeff Stapleton/CBC)

blocks.text: Manitoba·Updated

An embattled for-profit plasma centre in Winnipeg is now officially suspended from collecting the blood component, after Health Canada cited concerns about its "quality management" in the wake of a donor's death last year.
Company didn’t effectively implement 'corrective and preventive actions,' agency says

An embattled for-profit plasma centre in Winnipeg is now officially suspended from collecting the blood component, after Health Canada cited concerns about its "quality management system" in the wake of a donor's death last year.
The federal agency suspended Grifols's Taylor Avenue plasma centre licence "effective immediately," the regulator announced in an email Wednesday afternoon.

Advocates have been calling on the federal government to crack down on the company after CBC News reported two people died in the past year after donating plasma at Grifols clinics in Winnipeg, including the Taylor location.
Grifols had already temporarily shut down collection at the rest of its Canadian centres last month, citing "unfounded attention" on paid plasma collection in Canada.

"Grifols had not effectively implemented some corrective and preventive actions and, overall, it failed to demonstrate that the Taylor Avenue site has implemented an effective quality management system," Health Canada said Wednesday.
A spokesperson for the Spain-based company said the licence suspension has no impact on its current operations, since collection had already been paused.
The company is working with Health Canada on a reopening plan for its collection centres, the spokesperson said in an emailed statement sent Wednesday.
As of Sept. 1, the company has acquired full ownership of its Canadian operations, the spokesperson wrote, and since then it has been retraining staff and strengthening its procedures.
Grifols operates 17 centres in Canada that pay people for their plasma, including two in Winnipeg.
The now-suspended Taylor Avenue centre is where Rodiyat Alabede, 22, suffered a fatal cardiac arrest while donating plasma on Oct. 25, 2025.
"A temporary suspension is not enough," said Katherine Lanteigne, an advocate for Alabede and her family. She said she wants to see all Grifols sites across Canada suspended.
"Justice will not be served for Ms. Alabede and blood donors in Canada will not be safe if leadership at Grifols are not held accountable for their egregious safety violations."

items: Private clinic Grifols says it's pausing all plasma collection in Canada

blocks.text: The federal regulator initially inspected the Taylor Avenue site roughly a month after Alabede died and found multiple deficiencies it directed Grifols to fix.
After inspecting it twice more over the summer, Health Canada warned Grifols it could suspend the company's licence if the issues weren't addressed.
Health Canada said it proposed suspending Grifols's licence on Aug. 13 and gave the company "an opportunity to be heard."
That same day, Grifols announced it was pausing plasma collection at all of its Canadian locations. It described the pause as voluntary and proactive.
Before the pause and suspension, virtually all of Grifols's locations were already under the regulator's scrutiny.
After its head office in Oakville, Ont., failed an inspection, Health Canada slapped new terms and conditions on its licence for "recurring, systemic deficiencies" that applied to 16 of its centres.
The Winnipeg Innovation Drive site, officially known as Grifols Canada Plasma II Inc., was left out because it operates under a separate licence.
Health Canada said it will work with Grifols as it tries to restart operations and implement corrective action plans.
"Prior to resuming operations, Health Canada will verify Grifols's compliance with our regulatory requirements and we will not hesitate to take further action if needed," the agency's email said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Michelle Allan is an award-winning investigative journalist based in Winnipeg. She's worked with CBC Thunder Bay, CBC's national investigative unit, CBC Ottawa and ran a pop-up bureau in Kingston, Ont. She won a 2021 Canadian Association of Journalists national award for investigative reporting and was a finalist in 2023 and 2024. You can reach her at michelle.allan@cbc.ca.
